summary: This unit teaches you to plan and carry out the mechanical cutting of steel for fabrication work: sawing, abrasive cutting, shearing, punching and notching. At Level 3 you will work out cutting lists and stock, choose the best machine for each part, set up guillotines, ironworkers and saws correctly, isolate machines safely, check the parts against the drawing, keep the records, and lead and train the people in your team.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). It covers **mechanical cutting**: cutting metal with blades, teeth, abrasive discs, punches and dies, without melting it. The machines are the bandsaw, cold saw, abrasive cut-off saw, hacksaw, guillotine (power shear), ironworker, punch, nibbler and tube notcher.

Every fabrication job starts with cutting. A frame that is cut 2 mm short, a mitre that is out by a degree, or a blank with a torn edge causes trouble at fit-up and welding. At Level 3 you do more than operate a machine: you **plan the cutting**, choose the method, set the machine up, check the first parts, keep the team safe and keep records that prove the parts are right.

**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 3 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and fabricators who lead a small team in a workshop. You should already be able to use a tape, a square and the basic hand tools safely.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Read the drawing and cutting list, group the parts, fit them onto stock lengths or sheets, allow for kerf and squaring, and work out the stock and the offcuts.
Pick the saw, shear, punch or other tool that gives the edge quality, accuracy and speed the job needs, within the machine's limits.
Check guards and stops, control noise, dust, coolant and handling hazards, and lock off and prove a machine before anyone works on it.
Choose the blade pitch, speed and feed, set the length stop and the angle, use coolant, and read the chips and the cut.
Set up and run shears and punches
Check the rating, set blade clearance, hold-downs and back gauge, match punch and die, and work out the punching force.
Measure first-off and sample parts with the right tools, compare them with the tolerance, deburr and mark them, and deal with parts that do not conform.
Keep blades, coolant and machines in good order, log faults and blade changes, and sort offcuts and scrap.
Share out the work, train and supervise others, and keep cutting plans, inspection sheets and offcut registers.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on planning and calculations, choosing the method, sawing, shearing, punching, safety and isolation, health hazards, checking the work, maintenance and supervision.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact trade terms such as die, slug, set, kerf, cutting list) and longer answers that explain a method, a calculation or a safe system of work.

**Practical tasks** done as a team: planning, cutting and checking a full set of frame parts from a cutting list, and running a batch of sheared and punched blanks with inspection records. The assessor watches how you plan, set up, isolate, check and record, not only the finished parts.

blocks.note: Show your working in every calculation: the stock length, the allowance for squaring, the kerf for each cut, and the answer with its unit. Marks are given for the method as well as the answer.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Cutting machines do not tire and do not stop for fingers. Most serious injuries come from reaching into a machine that is still able to move: under a guillotine blade, past a bandsaw guard, or under a punch. The rules below apply to every machine in this unit.

head: Hazard
Where it comes from
How you control it
rows: Guillotine blades and hold-downs, punches, ironworker shears, saw blades, back gauges
Guards in place and working before use
Hands kept out of the danger zone; feed long work, not short scraps
One operator per machine; the person feeding the work controls the pedal
Never reach behind or under a machine that can move
Rotating blades, chucks and feed rollers catching gloves, sleeves, hair or rags
Close-fitting clothing, sleeves buttoned, hair tied back, no jewellery
No loose gloves near a turning blade; use a push stick or clamp
Wear cut-resistant gloves for handling sheet, not while feeding a turning blade
Chips, slugs, broken teeth, a shattering abrasive disc, offcuts thrown by a saw
Safety glasses always; face shield for abrasive cutting
Disc speed rating checked; stand to one side when starting
Work clamped; offcut free to fall clear
Abrasive cut-off saws (often 95–105 dB(A)), guillotines, punching, hammering
Hearing protection worn and signs up wherever noise is high
Loud work done away from others
Machines maintained so they run quietly
Abrasive cutting: steel and grit dust, and fume from paint or zinc coatings
Respirator where the risk assessment says
Clean up by vacuum or damp sweeping, never by blowing
Soluble oil coolant on saws: skin rashes (dermatitis) and oil mist, worse when it is old and dirty
Correct mix, changed when dirty or smelly
Gloves and barrier cream; wash before eating
6 m bars, full sheets and heavy offcuts
Sheet trolleys, lifting clamps, roller stands
Plan the lift; team lifts with one person giving the commands
Burrs, sheared edges, nibbler swarf, bandsaw chips
Swarf removed with a brush or hook, never bare hands
Sparks from abrasive saws landing in rags, cardboard or oily swarf
Cut away from anything that burns
Extinguisher at hand; check the area after cutting

blocks.p: Before anyone changes a blade, sets a clearance, clears a jam or reaches into any machine, the machine must be **isolated**, **locked off** and **proved dead**. Pressing the stop button is not isolation: someone can press start, a control fault can start it, and stored energy can still move it.

flow: Plan the job and tell everyone who uses the machine that it is being isolated
Stop the machine with its normal controls
Switch off at the main isolator (not the start/stop buttons)
Fit a multi-lock hasp; every person who will work on the machine fits their **own padlock and tag** with their name; each keeps their own key
Release or block **stored energy**: hydraulic or air pressure, a raised guillotine beam or bandsaw head, springs, a blade still coasting
**Prove** the isolation: with everyone clear, try the start button and the pedal; nothing must move; return the controls to off
Do the work
Refit guards, remove tools and rags, check everyone is clear
Each person removes only their own lock; test the machine before it goes back into use

blocks.note: Never remove another person's lock, and never ask someone to remove theirs for you. If a worker must leave before the job is finished, the Centre's handover procedure is followed: the person taking over fits their own lock before the first person removes theirs, so the machine is never left unlocked while someone is still exposed.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: A hydraulic guillotine or press brake stores energy in pressurised oil, and its heavy beam can drift down if a valve leaks. Switching off the motor does not remove that. Lower the beam to its rest position or block it with the maker's safety blocks, and release pressure as the maker's manual says, before you reach between the blades.

blocks.h: Your duties as a team leader

ul: Check that every team member has had the machine induction and wears the right PPE: safety glasses, hearing protection, safety boots, close-fitting clothing, and gloves suited to the task.
Check guards, hold-downs, stops and emergency stops before the run, and walk the area for trip hazards and loose bars.
Allow only trained people on each machine, one operator at a time.
Stop any unsafe act at once, explain why, and show the safe way. Do not wait for the end of the job.
Report and record injuries, near misses and damaged equipment, and tag faulty machines DO NOT USE.
Remember the heat: in a hot Jamaican workshop people tire and take short cuts. Plan water and rest breaks into a long cutting job.

sections.title: Planning the cutting and the calculations

blocks.p: Good cutting starts at the desk. A **cutting list** lists every part to be cut, with its part number, section, material, length or size, quantity and any angles. Check it against the drawing and its revision letter before anyone cuts: a list made from an old drawing gives a full set of wrong parts.

flow: Check the cutting list against the latest drawing and correct any mistakes with the supervisor
Group the parts by section and material (all the 50 × 50 tube together, all the angle, all the flat bar, all the plate blanks)
Measure the stock you actually have: most sections come in 6 m lengths, but some suppliers still sell 20 ft (about 6.1 m)
Fit the parts onto the stock lengths (nesting): longest parts first, then fill the gaps with shorter parts
Allow for squaring the mill end and for the kerf of every cut
Choose the machine for each group and share out the work, with one person checking first-off parts
Work out the bars or sheets needed and the offcuts, and record useful offcuts in the offcut register

blocks.p: The **kerf** is the width of material turned into chips or dust by a cut. Each saw cut loses about the width of the blade's set: often about 1.5–2.5 mm on a bandsaw, 2–3 mm on a cold saw and 3 mm or more with an abrasive disc. A guillotine or ironworker shear has no kerf. The mill end of a bar is often not square or is damaged, so allow a few millimetres (often 5–10 mm) to square it before the first part.
For planning, allow **one kerf for every part** you cut from the bar. The usable length is the bar length less the squaring allowance.

head: Step
Worked example: 9 pieces of 1 300 mm and 6 pieces of 700 mm from 6 m tube; kerf 3 mm; squaring 5 mm
rows: 5 995 ÷ 1 303 = 4.6, so 4 per bar (5 212 mm), leaving 783 mm
One 700 mm part fits in the 783 mm: 5 212 + 703 = 5 915 mm, leaving 80 mm
3 bars. The 1 880 mm piece is a useful offcut: label it with its size and grade and enter it in the offcut register.

blocks.note: Dividing the total length of parts by the bar length gives the least number of bars possible, not the number you need, because parts cannot be joined across two bars. Always lay the parts out bar by bar.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A frame with mitred corners has its rails cut at **45°** at both ends. Each rail then has a long edge (the **long point**, on the outside of the frame) and a short edge (the **short point**, on the inside). The difference between them is the depth of the section at each mitred end.

head: Frame of 40 × 40 mm tube, outside size 1 200 × 800 mm, 45° mitres at both ends
Long point (outside edge)
Short point (inside edge)

ul: Set the length stop to the point the drawing dimensions, usually the long point, and say so on the cutting plan so nobody measures the other edge.
If the mitre is at one end only, the difference is one section depth, not two.
A mitre that is out by 1° at each end leaves a 4° error at the corner of the frame: check the saw head angle with a protractor or bevel gauge on the first cut.

blocks.p: Sheet is commonly 1 220 × 2 440 mm (4 × 8 ft) or 1 250 × 2 500 mm. On a guillotine there is no kerf, so the number of strips is the sheet width divided by the strip width, rounded **down**.

ul: Strips of 150 mm from a 1 220 mm width: 1 220 ÷ 150 = 8.13, so **8 full strips** and a 20 mm strip of waste.
Blanks of 150 × 300 mm: 8 strips of 150 mm × 2 440 mm, each giving 2 440 ÷ 300 = 8.13, so 8 blanks; 8 × 8 = **64 blanks** per sheet.
Dividing the sheet area by the blank area (2 976 800 ÷ 45 000 = 66.2) gives too many, because the leftover strips are too small to use.

blocks.p: A **tolerance** is how far a size may be from the drawing size and still be accepted. The drawing or the cutting list gives it.

blocks.note: A one-sided tolerance such as +0 / −2 means the part may be shorter but never longer than the drawing size. Fabricators use it where a part must fit inside something.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: **Waste:** waste % = offcut length ÷ bar length × 100. A 300 mm offcut from a 6 000 mm bar is 5% waste.
**Time:** number of cuts × time per cut, plus set-up and checking time.
**Cost:** bars or sheets needed × price, in J$. Add a small allowance for a spoiled part on a big job.
**Units:** 1 kN = 1 000 N; 1 tonne-force ≈ 9.81 kN; 1 m = 1 000 mm.

blocks.p: At Level 3 you choose the method, not just use the machine in front of you. Ask: what is the material and section? How accurate and square must the cut be? Will the edge be welded, seen or handled? How many parts? Can the machine take this thickness and material?

head: Method
Best for
Edge and accuracy
Limits
rows: Bar, tube, angle, channel and beams; straight cuts and mitres; solid bar up to large sizes
Clean, square edge; small kerf; little heat; small burr
Needs the right blade pitch, speed, feed and coolant
Cold saw (circular, low speed, HSS or carbide-tipped blade)
Accurate, square cuts and mitres on tube and sections; repeat parts
Very clean, square, cool edge; small burr; accurate length
Blades are costly and must suit the material
Quick one-off cuts; hardened or awkward material
Hot, heat-tinted edge with a heavy burr; less square
Discs wear fast and can shatter
Small sections, conduit, cutting on site with no power
Square if done with care; slow
Slow and tiring on large sections
Straight cuts in sheet and plate; many blanks to size with the back gauge
Fast, no kerf, no swarf; rolled edge on one side and a burr on the other
Thickness and length limits; lower for stainless
Narrow strips can twist and bow
Shearing flat bar, angle and round or square bar; punching holes; notching corners
Fast; sheared edge with a burr; punched hole slightly tapered
Many holes or shapes in sheet and plate
Large force; tooling for each shape
Curves and cut-outs in sheet up to a few millimetres; cutting sheet already fixed in place
Slightly scalloped edge; small, sharp swarf
The curved 'fish-mouth' end that lets one round tube sit tight against another, at an angle
Close fit for welding handrails and frames
Each notcher suits a range of tube sizes

blocks.p: A **notch** is a piece cut out of the edge or end of a part, for example a V notch in the flange of an angle so it can be bent into a corner. **Coping** is cutting away part of the end of a beam so that it fits under or around the flange of another beam. Small notches are made on the ironworker's notcher; copes on heavy beams are usually sawn, or cut thermally and ground.

head: Job
Best choice
Why
rows: 200 identical 100 × 60 mm blanks from 3 mm sheet
Guillotine with the back gauge, first-off checked
Fast, no kerf, every blank the same size
Mitred frame of 40 × 40 mm tube for a display cabinet
Cold saw or bandsaw with the head set to 45°
Square, accurate, cool mitres that fit tight for welding
One length of 25 mm hardened bar for a repair
Saw blades will not cut hardened steel well
Twenty 14 mm holes in 6 mm flat bar
Fast; hole size is larger than the plate thickness
Large curved opening in 1.2 mm sheet already riveted to a frame
Follows a curve and works in place
Ends of 100 mm solid round bar for machining
Bandsaw or cold saw with coolant
Clean, square cut with no heat damage

blocks.note: A sheared or punched edge that will be welded must be straight, clean and free of a heavy burr and of oil. An abrasive-cut edge is hot and heavily burred: dress it before fit-up.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Sawing: bandsaws, cold saws, abrasive saws and hacksaws

head: Term
Meaning
rows: The spacing of the teeth, usually given in **teeth per inch (TPI)**. A coarse blade has few teeth per inch; a fine blade has many.
Tooth spacing that changes along the blade, for example 4/6 TPI. It cuts a range of sizes and sections with less vibration and noise.
The bending of the teeth alternately left and right, so the cut (kerf) is wider than the blade body and the blade does not bind.
The space in front of each tooth that carries the chips out of the cut.
High speed steel tooth edge welded to a tough spring-steel back; the usual production bandsaw blade.
High speed steel: blade or tooth material that stays hard when hot.
Teeth tipped with tungsten carbide, very hard and long-lasting; used on many cold saws and for hard or abrasive material.
How fast the teeth pass the work, given in **metres per minute (m/min)**.
How hard and how fast the blade is fed into the work.

blocks.p: The pitch must suit the **thickness of metal in the cut**, not the size of the section. Keep at least **three teeth** in the cut at all times so the teeth cannot snag on a thin wall. But on a long cut through solid bar, fine teeth fill their gullets with chips before they leave the cut: the blade stops cutting, rubs, heats up and wanders.

head: Material in the cut
Typical bandsaw pitch
Why
rows: Thin-wall tube or angle, 2–3 mm wall
Keeps three or more teeth on the thin wall, so they do not snag and strip
A balance of smooth cutting and chip room
Gullets big enough for the longer cut
Large gullets carry the chips out of a long cut

blocks.note: These are typical figures from blade makers' charts. Use the chart for the blade and machine you have, and ask your instructor.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Material
Typical bi-metal blade speed
Feed and coolant
rows: Firm, steady feed so the teeth cut and do not rub; plenty of coolant
Slower still, as the chart says
Much faster, where the saw allows
Lighter feed; coolant or lubricant to stop chips sticking

blocks.p: **Stainless steel work-hardens**: if a tooth rubs instead of cutting, the surface under it becomes harder, so the next tooth rubs more. Too high a speed makes heat that does the same. So stainless is cut at a lower blade speed but with a firm feed.

head: Chips look like
What it means
What to do
rows: Thin, tightly curled, silver or light gold
Thick, blue or dark brown, hot
Too much feed or too high a speed
Reduce the feed or the speed; check the coolant
Teeth rubbing: feed too light, or blade blunt
Increase the feed; check the blade
Pitch too fine for the cut

flow: Check the blade: right pitch and type, teeth pointing in the direction of travel, no missing teeth
Check the blade tension with the machine's gauge or as the maker says
Move the blade guide arms in as close to the work as the work allows
Set the vice angle (0° for square, 45° for mitres) and check it with a protractor
Support long bars on **roller stands** at the right height, with walkways kept clear
Set the length stop so the cut piece falls clear and is never trapped between the blade and the stop
Clamp the work firmly; thin tube may need packing so it is not crushed
Set speed and feed from the chart; turn on the coolant; cut
Check the first part for length, angle and squareness before cutting the rest

blocks.note: A **new blade** is run in for its first few cuts at a lighter feed (often about half) so that its very sharp tips are honed rather than chipped. This makes the blade last much longer. Follow the blade maker's run-in figures.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Fault
Likely causes
Cure
rows: Blade blunt or teeth damaged on one side
Guide arms set too far from the work
Pitch too fine for the cut
Pitch too coarse for a thin wall
Feed too heavy at the start of a cut
Tension too high or too low
Blade too thick for the wheel size
Speed and feed from the chart
Length stop set so the piece is caught between blade and stop
Set the stop so the piece falls clear, or back the stop off before the cut finishes

blocks.p: A cold saw uses a circular HSS or carbide-tipped blade turning slowly, with coolant (HSS) or as the maker says (carbide). It gives a cool, very clean, square cut with a small burr, so it is the best saw for accurate repeat parts and mitres in tube and sections. Use the blade and speed the maker gives for the material, keep the vice clean so parts sit square, and change or resharpen the blade when the cut becomes rough or noisy.

ul: Check that the disc is a cut-off disc of the right size, **rated for at least the saw's speed** (the rpm or m/s marked on it), in date and not cracked or chipped. Never fit a larger disc than the guard is made for.
Keep the guard on. Stand to one side and run a new disc at full speed for about a minute before you cut, so a faulty or out-of-true disc shows itself before it is loaded.
Let the disc reach full speed before every cut, and feed steadily without forcing or twisting it.
Expect heat, sparks, dust and a heavy burr. Wear a face shield over safety glasses and hearing protection, and keep anything that burns away from the spark stream.
Choose the pitch so at least three teeth are on the thinnest part: about 18 TPI for solid bar, 24 TPI for angle and thick tube, 32 TPI for thin-wall tube and conduit.
Fit the blade with the teeth pointing away from the handle (the saw cuts on the push stroke) and tension it firmly.
Use the full length of the blade with steady strokes, and ease off at the end of the cut.

blocks.p: Shearing cuts metal between two blades. The top blade presses the metal down past the bottom blade until it cracks through. It is fast, makes no kerf and no swarf, but the edge is not the same all through.

head: Zone of a sheared edge
What it looks like
rows: A small rounded edge on the side where the blade entered
A smooth, shiny band where the metal was cut cleanly; on a good cut, roughly a third of the thickness
A rough, dull band where the metal cracked through
A sharp raised lip on the side where the blade came out

head: Part
Its job
rows: Top blade on the beam, bottom blade on the table
Do the cutting; most blades have four cutting edges and can be turned
Clamp the sheet firmly before the blade reaches it, so it cannot move or lift
Keeps fingers out of the hold-down and blade area at the front
An adjustable stop behind the blade that sets the size of each piece
A fence at 90° to the blade that keeps the sheet square to the cut
Hold up wide sheet in front of the blade
Stops anyone reaching or walking into the back of the machine
Start the stroke; stop the machine

blocks.p: The **clearance** is the small gap between the top and bottom blades. It is set from the **maker's chart** for each thickness and material, often roughly 5–10% of the sheet thickness, and checked with feeler gauges with the machine isolated.

head: Clearance
Result
rows: Clean edge, a good burnish band and a small burr
Metal is dragged into the gap and torn: big rollover, rough fracture and a heavy burr; thin sheet may fold and jam
Blades rub: they wear fast, the force goes up and the edge may show a double shiny band

blocks.note: When one class cuts thick plate and the next cuts thin sheet, the clearance must be reset. A ragged, heavily burred edge on thin sheet is the first sign that it was not.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: The **rake** is the slope of the top blade along its length, often about 1–2.5°. With rake, the blade cuts a little at a time like scissors, so the force is much lower. More rake means less force but more **twist and bow in narrow strips**. Many hydraulic guillotines let you lower the rake for narrow strips; sharp blades, the right clearance and working hold-downs also help.

ul: The rating plate gives the largest thickness the machine can cut, usually in **mild steel**, and the full cutting length.

**Stainless steel** is much stronger, so the capacity is lower: many makers give about two-thirds of the mild steel figure. Softer aluminium may be allowed a little thicker. Always check the maker's figure for the material.
The thickness limit applies **whatever the width**: a narrow flat bar thicker than the rating must not be put through the guillotine. Use the ironworker's flat-bar station or a saw.
Never shear round bar, hardened material or welded joints on a guillotine, and never cut a piece too small for the hold-downs to grip.

flow: Check the material and thickness against the rating
Isolate, check the blades for chips and wear, and set the clearance from the chart
Check the guards, hold-downs, rear guard and emergency stops
Set the back gauge to the size; check the squaring arm is square to the blade
Cut a **first-off** piece and measure it; adjust the back gauge if needed and cut another
Run the batch, keeping the sheet against the squaring arm and the back gauge
Check samples during the run (for example every tenth piece) and after any change
Stack the blanks with care: sheared edges are sharp

head: Fault in sheared parts
Likely cause
Cure
rows: Reset clearance; turn or regrind blades
Blanks out of square (diagonals not equal)
Squaring arm out of square, or sheet not held against it
Check the arm with a large square; keep the sheet against it
Too much rake; blunt blades; wrong clearance
Lower the rake; sharp blades; correct clearance
Back gauge loose or not checked; sheet not pushed fully to the gauge; thin sheet sagging behind the blade
Lock and check the gauge; support thin sheet; check samples
Hold-downs not working or set too high
Report and repair; do not run without them

blocks.note: Never reach behind or under the blade while the guillotine is switched on: the beam can come down and trap your hand or arm. Collect blanks from the back only when the machine is isolated, or use the chute or tray made for them.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: An **ironworker** (universal steelworker) is a hydraulic machine with several stations: a **punch**, a **flat-bar shear**, an **angle shear**, a **bar shear** for round and square bar, and a **notcher**. Each station has its own capacity on the rating plate. Only one person operates it at a time, and the person feeding the work is the person who controls the pedal, so nobody's hand is in the tooling when the ram moves.

head: Part
Its job
rows: The hardened tool that is pushed through the plate
The hardened block under the plate, with a hole slightly larger than the punch
Holds the work down so the punch can pull out of it on the up-stroke; set just above the plate
The disc of metal pushed out of the hole into the die
Locate each hole at the same position on every part

ul: The die must be the one the maker's chart pairs with that punch size **for that plate thickness**: the gap between them grows as the plate gets thicker.
Punch and die must be lined up and tight. A die that is loose or out of line lets the punch strike its edge and break.
Check the punch tip for chips and the die for cracks before a run.

blocks.p: When a hole is punched, the metal is sheared all round the edge of the hole. The area being sheared is the **circumference of the hole × the plate thickness**, so:

blocks.note: **Force (N) = π × d × t × shear strength**, where d is the hole diameter in mm, t is the plate thickness in mm, and shear strength is in N/mm² (newtons per square millimetre).
blocks.label: Remember

head: Step
Worked example: a 16 mm hole in 8 mm mild steel, shear strength 300 N/mm²
rows: Compare with the punching capacity on the rating plate for mild steel; leave a margin

ul: Mild steel is often taken as about 300–350 N/mm² in shear. Stainless steel is much stronger (often about 450–500 N/mm²), so the same hole needs roughly 1.5 times the force. Use the figure your instructor or the data sheet gives.
If the force is near or above the rating, the punch, die or frame can break and pieces can fly. Choose a smaller hole, a thinner plate, a bigger machine, or drill the hole.

blocks.p: A punch pushing through plate thicker than its own diameter is very likely to buckle or snap. So a punched hole in mild steel should be **no smaller in diameter than the plate is thick** (a 12 mm hole is the smallest in 12 mm plate). Makers ask for a larger ratio in stainless and other strong steels. Holes smaller than this are drilled.

ul: A punched hole is slightly tapered: wider on the die side, with a shiny band at the top and a rougher band below.

The metal round the edge is **work-hardened** and can have tiny cracks. In thick plate or parts that carry heavy or repeated loads, an engineer's specification may forbid full-size punched holes, and ask for the holes to be drilled, or punched small and then reamed to size.
Space holes at least the distances the drawing gives from edges and from each other; a hole too close to an edge can tear out.

blocks.p: The notcher cuts a rectangular or V-shaped piece from the edge of flat bar or from the flange of angle, for example so an angle frame can be bent at the corner or two angles can be fitted together. Set the stops so every notch is the same, and keep fingers clear of the blades: notching pieces are small and close to the tooling.

head: Punching fault
Likely cause
Cure
rows: Hole smaller than plate thickness; punch and die not lined up; overload
Keep d ≥ t; line up and tighten; check the force
Work lifts with the punch and slams down
Stripper set too high or missing
Set the stripper just above the plate
Correct die from the chart; regrind or replace
Set and lock the stops; check the first-off part

sections.title: Checking the work, quality control and records

head: Tool
Reads to about
Use it for
rows: Lengths of bars and frames; check the hook is not bent or loose
Strip widths, hole sizes, close tolerances such as ±0.2 mm
Squareness of cut ends and blanks
About 1° (a vernier bevel protractor reads much finer)

blocks.note: Choose a tool that reads at least about ten times finer than the tolerance. A tape that reads to 1 mm cannot check ±0.2 mm.
blocks.label: Tip

flow: Before the run: list the key sizes and tolerances from the drawing, and check the measuring tools
**First-off:** measure the first part fully and have a second person check it; record it before the run starts
**In-process:** check samples at set intervals (for example every fifth or tenth part) and after any blade change, stop reset or jam
**Final:** check a sample of the finished parts, count them and check their marks
Record every check on the **inspection sheet**, with the date and names

blocks.p: The first-off check finds **set-up errors** (a stop set wrongly, a wrong angle) before a whole batch is wrong. Checks during the run catch slow changes: a blade wearing, a stop creeping, a gauge knocked. If parts start coming out the same amount wrong every time, look first at the **set-up**: the length stop, the back gauge, the angle, and how they were measured.
A part that does not meet the drawing is **non-conforming**. Do not hide it, mix it with good parts or 'fix' it without asking.

flow: Stop and find out how many parts are affected
Label each one (for example with a red REJECT tag) and set them apart in a quarantine area
Report to the supervisor with the measurements
Find and correct the cause before cutting goes on
The supervisor decides: rework (a long part may be cut again to size), accept with the customer's agreement, or scrap
Record what was found and what was done

ul: Remove burrs with a file, a deburring tool or a flap disc so the parts are safe to handle and sit tight at fit-up.
Edges that will be welded must be straight, clean and free of oil, heavy burr and coolant.
Mark each part with its part number (paint marker or stamp) as soon as it is cut and checked, so parts cannot be mixed up.

head: Record
What it holds
Why
rows: Groups, bar-by-bar layout, machines, who does what
Shows the stock needed and lets others follow the plan
First-off, sample and final checks, with sizes, dates and names
Proves the parts met the drawing
Size, section and grade of each useful offcut and where it is stored
Offcuts get used instead of new stock
What was wrong, how many, the cause and the decision
Stops the same mistake happening again
Blade changes, settings, faults and repairs
Plans maintenance and shows repeat faults

sections.title: Maintenance, clean-up and leading the team

ul: Only a **trained person**, with the machine isolated and locked off, changes and sets blades, punches and dies.
Turn or regrind guillotine blades when the edge gets ragged; never use a chipped blade.
Keep guide arms, rollers and vices clean of chips; lubricate as the maker says.
Check guards, hold-downs and emergency stops at the start of each session.
Tag any faulty machine DO NOT USE and report it at once; do not work round a fault by using another part of the blade or machine.

Soluble coolant is a mix of concentrate and water, often about 5–10% concentrate. Mix it as the maker says (add the concentrate to the water) and check the strength with a refractometer if the Centre has one.
Too weak: rust, poor cutting and germs growing. Too strong: waste and more skin trouble.
Old coolant goes dirty, oily and sour-smelling as bacteria grow in it. Drain, clean the sump and refill when the maker says or when it smells or looks bad.
Dispose of used coolant as the Centre's rules say, never down a drain or onto the ground.

blocks.p: Each machine has a log with its name, number and location, the routine checks and when they are due, and every blade change, setting, fault and repair, with the date and the name of the person. Before a big job, read the log: is the machine in date, are there open faults, is a blade due? Over time the log shows repeat faults and where money must be spent.

ul: Isolate the machines at the end of the session.
Remove chips and swarf with a brush or hook, never with bare hands or compressed air.
Keep **stainless steel, aluminium, copper and brass** offcuts and swarf separate from mild steel scrap: sorted scrap sells for more and stainless swarf must not contaminate mild steel stock.
Store useful offcuts by section and size, labelled, and enter them in the register.
Put slugs and small pieces in their bins, sweep the floor, and leave walkways clear.

head: Task
What a good team leader does
rows: Shares the cutting plan, gives each person a group of parts and a machine they are trained for, and names the checker
Explains the job, the hazards, the stops and the checks before anyone starts
Watches set-ups and first-offs; corrects unsafe acts at once
Teaches new users step by step and signs them off only when competent
Makes sure checks, offcuts and faults are written down; reports problems to the supervisor

flow: Check they have had the general machine induction and are wearing the right PPE
Explain the machine's parts, controls, guards and emergency stop
Explain the hazards and the capacity limits on the rating plate
Demonstrate a set-up and a cut, explaining each step
Let them do it while you stand beside them; correct them at once
Let them carry on under close supervision until they are competent
Sign and record the training; keep checking their work for a while

blocks.note: Many Jamaican fabrication shops are small, and one person may run the saw, the guillotine and the ironworker in the same day. Make sure every new worker or trainee is trained on each machine, not just told to 'watch and learn'.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can read a drawing and cutting list and check one against the other.
I can plan the cutting of parts onto stock lengths, allowing for squaring and kerf, and work out the bars needed and the offcuts.
I can work out long and short points of mitred parts, strips and blanks from a sheet, and the limits of a tolerance.
I can choose the best cutting method for a job and explain its edge quality and limits.
I can choose a bandsaw blade pitch, speed and feed for solid bar, thin-wall tube and stainless steel, and read the chips.
I can set up a bandsaw, cold saw and abrasive saw safely, with the length stop set so parts cannot be trapped.
I can explain blade clearance, rake, hold-downs, back gauge and capacity on a guillotine, and set one up.
I can match a punch and die, set the stripper, and work out the punching force and check it against the rating.
I can explain why punched holes must not be smaller than the plate thickness, and why some specifications ban them.
I can isolate, lock off, release stored energy and prove a machine dead, with several people working on it.
I can control noise, dust, coolant, manual handling and sharp-edge hazards.
I can plan and carry out first-off, in-process and final checks with the right tools, and record them.
I can deal with non-conforming parts correctly.
I can keep a machine log, look after coolant, sort scrap and keep an offcut register.
I can train and supervise a team member on a cutting machine.

terms: The adjustable stop behind a guillotine blade that sets the size of each piece
A saw blade with high speed steel teeth welded to a spring-steel back
The gap between the top and bottom blades of a shear, set for the thickness and material
The sharp raised lip left on the edge where a cutting tool came out
A circular saw with a slow-turning HSS or carbide-tipped blade that gives a cool, square cut
Cutting away the end of a beam so it fits under or around the flange of another beam
A list of every part to be cut, with section, material, size, quantity and angles
The hardened block under the work, with a hole slightly bigger than the punch
The first part of a batch, fully measured and checked before the rest are cut
The space in front of a saw tooth that carries the chips out
Clamps on a guillotine that grip the sheet before the blade cuts
Cutting off and locking off all energy to a machine so it cannot move
The width of material lost in a saw cut
Each worker fits their own lock and tag to the isolator before working on a machine
The longer edge of a mitred part
An angled cut, usually 45°, so two parts meet at a corner
Fitting parts onto stock lengths or sheets so that waste is low
A part that does not meet the drawing or specification
A record of useful offcuts, their size, grade and where they are kept
The spacing of saw teeth, often given in teeth per inch (TPI)
The slope of a guillotine's top blade along its length
Saw teeth bent alternately left and right so the cut is wider than the blade
The disc of metal pushed out when a hole is punched
The part that holds the work down as the punch lifts out
How far a size may differ from the drawing size and still be accepted
A blade whose tooth spacing changes along its length
Metal becoming harder where it is rubbed or deformed, as stainless steel does under a rubbing tooth

c1.title: Market-stall frames for a municipal corporation in Linstead
c1.text: Shanice, a Level 3 trainee, leads a team cutting parts for 10 steel market stalls ordered by a municipal corporation in Linstead, St Catherine. Each stall needs 4 legs at 2 100 mm and 4 top rails of 1 450 mm (long point), all in 40 × 40 × 3 mm square tube; the rails have 45° mitres at both ends and form a square frame 1 450 × 1 450 mm outside. The tube comes in 6 m lengths. The cold saw's kerf is 3 mm, the team allows 10 mm to square each mill end, and the drawing allows ±1 mm on every length.

c2.title: Bracket blanks on the guillotine in Bog Walk
c2.text: A shop in Bog Walk, St Catherine, must cut 300 blanks, 120 × 60 mm, from 2.5 mm mild steel sheets of 1 220 × 2 440 mm, on a hydraulic guillotine rated for 6 mm mild steel. Yesterday another team cut 6 mm plate on it. This morning the first blanks have a ragged edge with a heavy burr, and some blanks are slightly out of square: their diagonals differ by 2 mm. A customer also asks whether 50 × 10 mm flat bar can be cut on the guillotine, 'since it is so narrow'.

c3.title: Punching base plates in Morant Bay
c3.text: Devon leads a small team in Morant Bay, St Thomas, making 60 base plates for street-light poles. Each plate is 12 mm mild steel with four 22 mm holes. The ironworker's punching capacity is 60 tonnes (about 590 kN) in mild steel. The team takes the shear strength of the plate as 350 N/mm². Jodi, a new trainee, is using the ironworker for the first time, and on the first plates the work lifts with the punch on the up-stroke and then slams back down.

c4.title: Bandsaw trouble in Savanna-la-Mar
c4.text: At a shop in Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland, the horizontal bandsaw has a 6/10 TPI bi-metal blade, fitted last week for 40 × 40 × 3 mm tube. Today Kemoy must cut 75 mm solid mild steel bar and some 50 mm stainless steel bar for pump shafts. On the 75 mm bar the cut is slow and the gullets are packed with chips. On the stainless bar the blade squeals and the chips come off as fine powder. Later, after fitting a new coarse blade, he cuts more mild steel bar with the feed turned well up to save time, and the chips come off thick, blue and very hot.

c5.title: A jam on the guillotine at the Centre in St Ann's Bay
c5.text: At the training centre in St Ann's Bay, St Ann, a blank has jammed between the blades of the hydraulic guillotine. Mr Henry, the workshop technician, and Tanisha, the Level 3 team leader, will free it. Both have fitted their own padlocks to the isolator hasp and proved the machine dead. Halfway through, Mr Henry is called away to another campus. When the jam is cleared, Tanisha finds a small chip in one end of the top blade.

questions.q: Shanice plans to cut two legs and one top rail from each 6 m bar. Allowing for squaring and a kerf for every part, how long is the offcut from each of these bars?
o: 331 mm
341 mm
340 mm
questions.why: Usable length 6 000 − 10 = 5 990 mm; each leg uses 2 103 mm and each rail 1 453 mm, so 5 990 − 4 206 − 1 453 = 331 mm. Leaving out the squaring gives 341 mm, leaving out the kerfs gives 340 mm, and 1 784 mm forgets the rail.

questions.q: She cuts all 40 legs on bars of two legs and one rail each, then cuts the remaining rails four to a bar. How many 6 m bars must she order?
o: 24 bars
25 bars
30 bars
20 bars
questions.why: Twenty bars give 40 legs and 20 rails; the other 20 rails at four per bar need 5 more bars, so 25. Dividing the total length of parts by 6 m (about 24) gives the theoretical least, but parts cannot be joined across bars.

questions.q: A trainee sets the length stop so that each top rail measures 1 450 mm along its inside (short) edge. What will be wrong with the frames?
o: Each side will be 40 mm too short on the outside
The sizes will be right, as the two mitres cancel out
Each side will be 80 mm too long on the outside
Each side will be 40 mm too long on the outside
questions.why: With 45° mitres at both ends, the long point is the short point plus two section depths: 1 450 + (2 × 40) = 1 530 mm, 80 mm over the drawing. Say on the plan which edge the stop is set to.

questions.q: The first-off leg measures 2 101.5 mm. What should Shanice do?
o: Accept it, as the error is far less than the tube's wall thickness
Cut the whole batch, then trim any long legs at the end of the day
Ask the welder to make it up at fit-up by leaving a wider root gap
Reset the length stop, then cut and check another first-off part
questions.why: The limits are 2 099–2 101 mm, so 2 101.5 mm is outside the tolerance. A first-off error is a set-up error: correct the stop and prove it on a new first-off before running the batch. A long part can often be re-cut to size.

questions.q: What is the most likely cause of the ragged edges and heavy burr on this morning's blanks, and the right first action?
o: Blunt blades; turn the blades round at the next planned service
Clearance still set for 6 mm; isolate and reset it from the chart
Too much rake on the top blade; lower the rake and carry on cutting
Sheet too soft; ask the store for a harder grade of mild steel
questions.why: A clearance set for 6 mm plate is far too large for 2.5 mm sheet, so the metal is dragged into the gap and torn. Isolate the machine and set the clearance for 2.5 mm from the maker's chart, checking it with feeler gauges.

questions.q: Each sheet is first cut into 120 mm strips across its 1 220 mm width, and the strips are then cut into 60 mm blanks. How many full blanks does one sheet give?
questions.why: 1 220 ÷ 120 = 10.2, so 10 strips, each 2 440 mm long; 2 440 ÷ 60 = 40.7, so 40 blanks per strip; 10 × 40 = 400. Dividing the areas gives 413, and 10 × 40.7 gives 406: both count part-blanks that cannot be used.

questions.q: Some blanks are out of square, with diagonals 2 mm different. What should be checked first?
o: The blade clearance, checked with a set of feeler gauges
The rake angle set on the top blade of the beam
The oil level in the guillotine's hydraulic tank
The squaring arm, and the sheet held against it
questions.why: Out-of-square blanks come from the sheet not being square to the blade: a squaring arm knocked out of true, or the sheet not pushed against it. Check the arm with a large square and cut a new first-off.

questions.q: What is the right answer to the customer about cutting the 50 × 10 mm flat bar on this guillotine?
o: Yes, because a narrow bar needs far less force than a full-width sheet
No: 10 mm is over its rating at any width; use the ironworker or a saw
Yes, as long as the rake is lowered and the bar is fed in very slowly
No: guillotines are only made for cutting sheet thinner than about 3 mm
questions.why: The rating is a thickness limit whatever the width, and overloading can damage the blades and the machine. The ironworker's flat-bar station (within its rating) or a saw is the right tool.

questions.q: Devon checks each 22 mm hole against the ironworker's 60-tonne rating. Roughly what force does one hole need?
o: About 92 kN
About 145 kN
About 290 kN
About 580 kN
questions.why: Force = π × d × t × shear strength = 3.142 × 22 × 12 × 350 = 290 300 N, about 290 kN (roughly 30 tonnes), well within the 590 kN rating. Leaving out π gives 92 kN; using the radius gives 145 kN.

questions.q: Devon fits a 22 mm punch. Which check on the die matters most before the first hole?
o: That it is the die the chart gives for that punch in 12 mm plate
That its hole is exactly 22 mm, the same size as the punch tip
That it has been warmed up with a gas torch so it is less brittle
That it is well greased so that the slugs can drop out of it easily
questions.why: The die hole must be a little bigger than the punch, and the right gap depends on the plate thickness, so use the die the maker's chart gives. It must also be tight and lined up, or the punch can strike its edge and break.

questions.q: Jodi wants to hold the small plates in place at the punch while Devon works the foot pedal. What should Devon say?
o: Yes, as two people make the job both faster and safer
Yes, as long as Jodi wears thick leather gloves
No: the person placing the work controls the pedal
No: small plates must be held in a vice under the punch
questions.why: When one person places the work and another works the pedal, the ram can come down while a hand is still in the tooling. One operator at a time: the person feeding the work controls the pedal and keeps hands clear.

questions.q: Why does the plate lift with the punch and slam back down, and what is the cure?
o: The stripper is set too high; lower it to just above the plate
The die is too large; fit a die exactly the same size as the punch
The punch is blunt; turn the machine's hydraulic pressure up to full
The plate is too thin; put two plates through the punch together
questions.why: The stripper holds the work down so the punch can pull out of it. If it is set too high, the plate rides up on the punch and drops back, which is a danger to hands and spoils the hole positions.

questions.q: Why is the 6/10 TPI blade cutting the 75 mm solid bar slowly?
o: Its teeth are too coarse to cut solid bar cleanly
Its fine teeth fill their gullets in so long a cut
Its blade speed is set far too low for mild steel bar
It needs much more coolant to wash the chips away
questions.why: On a long cut through solid bar each tooth makes more chips than a fine-pitch gullet can carry, so the gullets pack and the blade rubs and slows. A coarse pitch such as 3/4 TPI suits 75 mm bar.

questions.q: On the stainless bar the blade squeals and the chips are fine powder. What should Kemoy change?
o: Raise the blade speed so the teeth cut much faster
Turn the coolant off so that the teeth can grip better
Increase the feed so the teeth cut and do not rub
Lighten the feed further to protect the blade's teeth
questions.why: Powdery chips mean the teeth are rubbing, and rubbing work-hardens stainless steel so it gets harder to cut. Stainless needs a lower blade speed but a firm, steady feed, with plenty of coolant.

questions.q: What do the thick, blue, very hot chips from the later cuts tell Kemoy?
o: The blade is cutting well, as fast as it safely can
The pitch is still too fine for the solid mild steel bar
The teeth are rubbing, so the feed should go up further
The feed or blade speed is too high and must come down
questions.why: Good chips are thin, curled and silver or light gold. Thick, blue, hot chips mean too much feed or speed, which overheats and quickly wears the new blade. Powdery chips would mean rubbing; packed gullets would mean too fine a pitch.

questions.q: Mr Henry must leave before the job is finished. What should happen to his padlock?
o: Tanisha removes it with his key once he has left the building
He leaves his lock on and takes its key with him to the other campus
A person taking over fits their own lock before his is removed
He removes his own lock, since Tanisha's lock still protects the job
questions.why: Each person is protected only by their own lock. Under a handover procedure, the person taking over fits their own lock first, then Mr Henry removes his, so nobody working on the machine is left unprotected and no one removes another's lock.

questions.q: A trainee says the chip is only at one end of the blade, so the class can keep cutting at the other end. What should Tanisha do?
o: Agree, but tell the class to keep well away from the chipped end
Tag the guillotine out of use, record it and get the blade seen to
File the chip smooth herself so that the class can carry on cutting
Agree, as long as only thin sheet is cut until the next service is due
questions.why: A chipped blade gives poor cuts and the chip can spread or break off. Tag the machine DO NOT USE, record the fault in the machine log and report it, so a trained person turns, regrinds or replaces the blade and resets the clearance.

questions.q: Trevor must cut 20 mm electrical conduit with a 1.5 mm wall by hand. Which hacksaw blade should he fit?
o: 32 TPI, so at least three teeth are on the thin wall
14 TPI, so that each tooth takes a bigger, faster bite
18 TPI, the usual blade for cutting solid mild steel bar
24 TPI, fitted with the teeth pointing towards the handle
questions.why: At least three teeth must be in contact with the thinnest part, or they snag and strip on the wall. A 32 TPI blade suits thin-wall tube and conduit; the teeth point away from the handle so the saw cuts on the push stroke.

questions.q: A drawing gives a length of 750 +0 / −2 mm. Which measured part is acceptable?
questions.why: The part may be up to 2 mm short but never longer than 750 mm, so the accepted range is 748–750 mm. Only 748.5 mm is inside it.

questions.q: A new 355 mm disc is to be fitted to the abrasive cut-off saw. Which check matters most before it is fitted?
o: That the disc is thick enough to last the whole job
That its marked top speed is at least the saw's speed
That it is the same colour and make as the last one
That it has been soaked in coolant to cut more cleanly
questions.why: A disc run faster than its rating can burst with great force. Check that its marked speed is at least the saw's, that it is the right type and size for the guard, and that it is not cracked or out of date.
